data.title: SNAP-V: A RISC-V SoC with Configurable Neuromorphic Acceleration for Small-Scale Spiking Neural Networks
data.summary: A RISC-V neuromorphic SoC with two accelerator variants, Cerebra-S (bus-based) and Cerebra-H (NoC-based), optimised for small-scale SNN inference at 1.05 pJ per synaptic operation.

sections.heading: Abstract
body: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have gained significant attention in edge computing due to their low power consumption and computational efficiency. However, existing implementations either use conventional System on Chip (SoC) architectures that suffer from memory-processor bottlenecks, or large-scale neuromorphic hardware that is inefficient and wasteful for small-scale SNN applications.

This work presents SNAP-V, a RISC-V-based neuromorphic SoC with two accelerator variants: Cerebra-S (bus-based) and Cerebra-H (Network-on-Chip (NoC)-based), which are optimized for small-scale SNN inference. It integrates a RISC-V core for management tasks, with both accelerators featuring parallel processing nodes and distributed memory.

Experimental results show close agreement between software and hardware inference, with an average accuracy deviation of 2.62% across multiple network configurations, and an average synaptic energy of 1.05 pJ per synaptic operation (SOP) in 45 nm CMOS technology. These results show that the proposed solution enables accurate, energy-efficient SNN inference suitable for real-time edge applications.

sections.heading: Accelerator variants
list: Cerebra-S: a bus-based accelerator for the smallest network configurations
Cerebra-H: a Network-on-Chip based accelerator that scales across parallel processing nodes
A RISC-V management core handling configuration, orchestration and I/O
Distributed local memory at each processing node, avoiding the memory-processor bottleneck

sections.heading: Results
list: Average accuracy deviation of 2.62% between software and hardware inference
Average synaptic energy of 1.05 pJ per synaptic operation (SOP) in 45 nm CMOS
Validated across multiple network configurations

data.title: On-Chip Offline Neuromorphic Computing
data.summary: A custom RISC-V CPU with a six-instruction ISA extension for on-chip spiking neural network backpropagation training, running without any host PC.

sections.heading: Overview
body: A custom RISC-V CPU with a six-instruction ISA extension for on-chip spiking neural network (SNN) backpropagation training.
The target system is a three-stage on-chip learning loop: forward inference, surrogate-gradient substitution, and backpropagation weight updates, running entirely on the device without any host PC.

sections.heading: The learning loop
list: Forward inference across the spiking network
Surrogate-gradient substitution, making the non-differentiable spike function trainable
Backpropagation weight updates applied in hardware

data.title: On-Chip Online Learning for Neuromorphic Hardware
data.summary: Learning rules implemented directly in neuromorphic hardware, so a deployed device can adapt online without a round trip to a host machine.

sections.heading: Overview
body: This project implements learning directly within neuromorphic hardware, so that weight updates happen on the device rather than off-line on a host machine.
Moving the update path into hardware removes the retrain-and-reflash round trip, which matters for deployments that must adapt to a changing environment with no link back to a host.

sections.heading: Research questions
list: Which learning rules retain accuracy once quantised to a hardware-realisable weight representation?
What is the area and energy cost of an on-chip update path relative to inference-only silicon?
How should local synaptic state be organised so updates do not serialise on memory access?

data.title: Memory and Power Optimization in Neuromorphic Accelerators
data.summary: Attacking the dominant bottleneck in neuromorphic hardware: distributed memory inefficiency and the energy cost of moving synaptic state.

sections.heading: Overview
body: This project investigates memory and power optimization techniques for neuromorphic accelerators, addressing one of the key bottlenecks in modern neuromorphic hardware: distributed memory inefficiency and energy constraints.

In practice, a large share of the energy in a neuromorphic accelerator is spent not on computing neuron updates but on fetching and writing back synaptic state. The work targets that traffic directly, through memory organisation and access scheduling rather than through changes to the neuron model.

data.title: PeraMorphIQ SRAM Compiler
data.summary: An OpenRAM-based SRAM compiler for generating custom memory macros, with automated output organisation, two-dimensional banking and Synopsys tool integration.

sections.heading: Overview
body: The PeraMorphIQ SRAM Compiler is a production-ready tool for generating custom SRAM macros. It provides a simplified workflow on top of OpenRAM with improved stability, automated output organisation, and integrated post-processing for industry-standard design flows.
Distributed under the BSD-3-Clause licence and built on OpenRAM (Regents of the University of California, Santa Cruz).

sections.heading: Improvements over base OpenRAM
list: Stability fixes: resolved circular imports in sram_factory and globals.py
Modern compatibility: works with NumPy 1.20 and above
Automated organisation of every generated artefact into a predictable directory tree
Two-dimensional banking, adding a mixed mode alongside vertical and horizontal
Synopsys integration: scripted .lib to .db compilation and ICC2 NDM generation

sections.heading: Banking modes
body: All three modes are the same arithmetic over an (h, v) array shape, where h slices the word width and v divides the address space.
list: Vertical: the address space is divided across banks, one bank active per access, lowest power
Horizontal: the word width is bit-sliced across banks, all banks accessed in parallel, no bank-mux latency
Mixed: both axes at once, for wide words in deep arrays where either single-axis split would exceed a practical macro size

sections.heading: Supported technologies
list: FreePDK45 (45 nm predictive PDK)
Sky130 (SkyWater open-source PDK)
GF180MCU (GlobalFoundries mixed-signal PDK)
scn4m_subm and scn3me_subm (MOSIS scalable CMOS)

sections.heading: Outputs
list: GDSII layout and LEF abstracts for place and route
Liberty timing libraries across multiple PVT corners
Verilog behavioural models and SPICE netlists
HTML datasheets, plus compiled .db and ICC2 NDM libraries when Synopsys tools are available

data.title: Neuromorphic NoC Architecture for Spiking Neural Networks
data.summary: A RISC-V Network-on-Chip with custom accelerator hardware, supporting up to 1,024 neurons on an FPGA with dedicated FIFO buffers for stable, low-power operation.

sections.heading: Abstract
body: The present works of AI show interest in trying to replicate some aspect of brain function. This interest stems from the fact that the brain remains functionally superior to any machine built to date despite consuming power equivalent to that of a compact fluorescent light bulb.

Spiking Neural Network (SNN), a type of artificial neural network, draws inspiration from the brain and uses spikes as the basis for communication in an event-driven manner. Spiking hardware, or neuromorphic hardware, is used to implement spike-based algorithms to realise their efficiency in computing and their ability to do so with low power, compared to non-spiking hardware.

Our research presents the design of a scalable and configurable Network-on-Chip (NoC) based on the RISC-V instruction set architecture (ISA) which allows for hardware-level processing of spiking neural networks, and the implementation of the design on an FPGA. RISC-V was chosen as the base ISA since it is not only highly practical and popular, but also completely open source and amenable to custom extensions.
The main goal of this research is to optimise the RISC-V processing node network for low power by integrating custom accelerator hardware units.

sections.heading: Related work
body: Spiking neural networks fall in the category of artificial neural networks, and represent a newer variant considered to be a third-generation neural network. They resemble the activities of the brain more closely by incorporating time, transmitting spikes as events throughout the network. When a synapse receives an action potential from one of its pre-synaptic neurons, it transmits the spike to its post-synaptic neurons, updating the membrane potential according to the synaptic weight and other neuron parameters.

Intel's Loihi adopts a variation of the CUBA leaky-integrate-and-fire model, featuring a manycore mesh of 128 neuromorphic cores connected by an asynchronous NoC that transports all communication as packetized messages. Each core implements 1,024 spiking neural units sharing configuration and state across ten architectural memories.

The OpenSpike project and related ASIC work demonstrate application-specific implementations of the leaky integrate-and-fire model with time-multiplexed accelerator designs. SpiNNaker, by contrast, focuses on scale, simulating aggregates of up to a billion neurons in real time using nodes of 18 ARM968 cores each with 128 MB of off-die SDRAM.

sections.heading: Methodology
body: The proposed design consists of RISC-V processing nodes specialised to perform the operations required to implement spiking networks. The nodes are interconnected using a network interface attached to each processing node, with a routing framework negotiating communication between them. Each processing node is responsible for managing one or more logical neurons, and the interconnectivity enables communication between logical neurons that span multiple nodes. The architecture adopts an event-driven messaging mechanism to emulate the activity of spiking neurons.

The motivation for using a RISC-V processing node network lies in the ability to maintain configurability and programmability at the hardware level. This flexibility is leveraged to support various spiking neuron model architectures.

images.caption: Overall architecture of the neuromorphic NoC.
Single neuron implementation within a processing node.

sections.heading: Experiment setup and implementation
body: Once the architecture was completed and verified in simulation, it was implemented on an FPGA device, specifically the Altera DE2-115. A small-scale SNN was then tested on the device to confirm the implementation.

The number of neurons the design can simulate was restricted to 1,024, chosen to support that count efficiently in both power and time. An SNN with 994 neurons was successfully simulated on the design for MNIST classification.

An architectural experiment was conducted to quantify the benefit of using multiple FIFO buffers at the output side of the neuron interconnect. The objective was to observe the difference in operating frequency between a single shared FIFO buffer and dedicated FIFO buffers from the neuron interconnect to the neurons, which established the right balance between resource usage and time efficiency.

images.caption: Small-scale SNN mapped onto the FPGA.
FIFO buffer circuit at the neuron interconnect output.

sections.heading: Results and analysis
body: The operating frequency declines sharply as the number of neurons increases when a single FIFO buffer is placed at the output of the network interconnect leading to the accumulator units. With dedicated FIFO buffers for each accumulator unit, the frequency remains relatively stable, showing only minor variation. This stability is attributed to the absence of bottlenecks as the system scales.

images.caption: Operating frequency against neuron count, single versus dedicated FIFO buffers.

sections.heading: Conclusion
body: While there are designs that facilitate large-scale architectures, there is a scarcity of designs that fully exploit programming flexibility. By targeting small-scale SNNs, this design introduces considerable flexibility through the combination of a general-purpose RISC-V processor and a custom accelerator. Although it does not match the scale of large architectures, it is optimised for applications that rely on small-scale SNNs, prioritising performance and low power consumption.

data.title: RV32IMF Neuromorphic Network-on-Chip with Neuron Banks
data.summary: Customised RV32IMF RISC-V cores, a 2D mesh NoC and dedicated neuron-bank hardware, with event-driven spike communication via custom ISA extensions and AXI interfaces.

sections.heading: Abstract
body: Neuromorphic engineering endeavours to emulate the intricate functioning of the human brain through very large-scale integrated (VLSI) circuits. These architectures employ artificial neurons and synapses to replicate the characteristics of the brain, including its exceptional parallelism, rapid processing and energy efficiency, achieved by virtue of a densely interconnected neural network and its event-driven nature.

This work presents a Network-on-Chip (NoC) architecture based on the RISC-V instruction set architecture which allows for hardware-level processing of spiking neural networks, implemented and evaluated on an FPGA. RISC-V was chosen as the base ISA since it is highly practical and popular, completely open source, and amenable to custom extensions.

The design consists of customised RISC-V processing nodes interconnected using a network interface attached to each node, together with a routing framework to negotiate communication between nodes. Each processing node manages one or more neurons, and the architecture adopts an event-driven messaging mechanism to emulate neuron activity.

The primary objective is to demonstrate how a general-purpose ISA such as RISC-V can be augmented to perform a highly specialised task (the simulation of spiking neural networks in a scalable and configurable manner) whilst maintaining adherence to the original specifications of the ISA.

sections.heading: Related work
body: SpiNNaker, developed at the University of Manchester, utilises a network of 57,600 nodes each consisting of 18 ARM968 cores, and serves as the neuromorphic platform for the Human Brain Project. It uses a globally asynchronous locally synchronous routing mechanism for energy-efficient inter-node communication. While it boasts high performance and parallelism, it is an extremely expensive, large-scale project requiring 100 kW of power and an air-conditioned environment.

DYNAP (Dynamic Neuromorphic Asynchronous Processor) is a processor architecture with heterogeneous memory structures for minimising memory utilisation, focusing on the interconnect between processor nodes and proposing a hierarchical routing mechanism for efficient event-based communication.

The ODIN coprocessor targets SNN workloads in IoT applications through a reconfigurable neuromorphic coprocessor interfacing with a RISC-V SoC over SPI, allowing the RISC-V core to configure and offload SNN tasks. POETS is a customisable hardware platform for event-driven parallel programming, including a hyperthreaded RISC-V core named Tinsel designed to reduce latency.

Although numerous neuromorphic architectures exist, there is a lack of designs that exploit the programming flexibility and platform maturity of existing architectures. A neuromorphic architecture based on RISC-V, offering greater flexibility, yields a valuable compromise.

sections.heading: Methodology
body: The project proceeds by building a RISC-V core and adding custom hardware to handle SNN-related calculations, all implemented as a Network-on-Chip architecture. Verification is performed in both software and hardware, followed by simulation of an SNN on the designed architecture and evaluation of its performance.
list: Build the RISC-V core
Add custom hardware for spike calculation
Implement the Network-on-Chip
Verify in software and hardware
Simulate a spiking neural network
Evaluate performance

sections.heading: The core
body: The core is an RV32IMF implementation built to specification, handling the integer, multiplication and floating-point operations needed for SNN simulation. An interrupt mechanism handles communication with the network interface connected to the core, and additional ISA extensions cover NoC operations and spike calculations.

sections.heading: The Network-on-Chip
body: The NoC is a 2D mesh architecture where each core connects to a router through a local port.

The network interface is the primary means for a core to connect to the network. It includes an AXI4-slave protocol for better latency and bandwidth handling, making it a more general-purpose interface. Access from the core uses the custom instructions SWNET and LWNET, where LWNET is used exclusively by the interrupt service routine, triggered when the read buffer rises above a threshold.

For packet processing, flit handling converts packets from the core into flits and flits from the network into packets. This module is followed by an asynchronous FIFO buffer to handle data pass-through between two clock domains.

The input module to a router contains the input router that decides routing per flit, plus virtual channel buffers that provide deadlock freedom and resolve head-of-line blocking; a round-robin arbiter chooses the channel used for flit input. The output module similarly holds a set of virtual channels acting as a flow-control mechanism. The router itself is a large crossbar switch connecting each input module to each output module, with control signals generated from the collected input-module arbiter selections.

images.caption: Core-to-router connection in the 2D mesh NoC.
Router input module with virtual channel buffers.

sections.heading: Custom hardware: neuron banks
body: The neuron banks are specialised custom hardware designed to handle neuron update calculations away from CPU mediation. At the start of operation, neuron configuration parameters are set by the CPU. Spike calculation inputs are taken into an input buffer together with a random number generated at that instant, and these values are used in the neuron update calculation.

In the final architecture, the NoC is responsible for initialisation and spike calculation, while the neuron bank section performs continuous neuron updates and the neuron reset after a spike. Each core is allocated a section of the neuron banks for its own use, which defines the neuron-to-CPU mapping.

sections.heading: Experiments
body: Experiments were simulated on FPGA hardware across three configurations (a single core, a two-core NoC, and a two-core NoC with neuron banks), measuring the clock cycles taken to execute one second of simulation at 1 ms timesteps. The test network was a four-neuron fully connected network with weights.

Experiment I used a single core for the simulation of all neurons. Experiment II used two cores connected through the NoC, with the four neurons divided two per core. Experiment III used the same two cores but offloaded the neuron update calculation to the neuron bank, leaving only spike calculation and initialisation to the CPUs.

sections.heading: Results and analysis
body: The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed neuromorphic NoC architecture for SNN simulation. Performance improvements were observed with the multi-core NoC configuration and, more markedly, with the addition of custom neuron banks.

images.caption: Experimental results across the three configurations.

data.title: Neuromorphic Architecture with Parallel RISC-V Processing Elements
data.summary: Parallel RISC-V processing elements modelling spiking neurons individually or virtually grouped, with encoder and decoder modules for benchmarking on classical machine learning tasks.

sections.heading: Abstract
body: Neuromorphic architectures are hardware architectures that use biologically inspired neural functions as the basis of operation. Information processing based on spiking neuron architectures has attracted considerable attention in recent years due to its low power consumption compared to traditional artificial neural networks.

In the first stage of this project, parallel multiple processing elements based on the RISC-V architecture are implemented to represent biological neurons. A single neuron can be implemented as a single processor with local memory access; alternatively, since the spike time of biological neurons is on the order of milliseconds, multiple neurons can be virtualised onto a single processor.
At the second stage, encoders and decoders are designed to benchmark the architecture by solving classical machine learning problems.

sections.heading: Technical approach
body: Given that biological neurons operate with spike times in the millisecond range, the architecture supports virtualisation where multiple neurons are efficiently managed by a single processor. This optimises resource utilisation while maintaining the temporal characteristics essential to neuromorphic computation.

Each processing element is designed with local memory access, ensuring low-latency data retrieval and storage. This distributed memory approach aligns with the decentralised nature of biological neural networks and contributes to the overall energy efficiency of the system.

The architecture is specifically optimised for spiking neural networks, which process information through discrete spike events rather than continuous signals. This event-driven model leads to significant power savings, especially where neural activity is sparse.

sections.heading: Research goals
list: Develop efficient parallel processing elements based on the RISC-V architecture
Implement neuron virtualisation techniques for optimal resource utilisation
Create encoders and decoders for machine learning applications
Benchmark the architecture against classical machine learning problems
Demonstrate significant power savings compared to traditional neural networks

sections.heading: Applications
body: The neuromorphic architecture developed in this project has potential applications across several domains: low-power neural processing for IoT devices at the edge; real-time decision making with minimal energy consumption in autonomous systems; efficient processing of visual and auditory signals; neural signal processing for brain-computer interfaces; and adaptive behaviour and learning in robotics.
